t.7.22.1: But Yama, son of Vivasvat, hearing that mighty roar of his, judged his enemy to be victorious and his own army destroyed.
t.7.22.2: But he, thinking his warriors slain, his eyes agitated with rage, quickly said to his charioteer, "Let the chariot be brought up!"
t.7.22.3: His charioteer brought up the divine, loudly rumbling chariot and stood ready, and that one of great splendour mounted the great chariot.
t.7.22.4: And before him stood Mṛtyu, noose and mallet in hand, by whom the whole of the three worlds, with all that moves and does not move, is drawn in and destroyed.
t.7.22.5: And Kāladaṇḍa, Yama's divine weapon, stood embodied in the chariot at his side, as if blazing with fiery splendor.
t.7.22.6: Then the three worlds were terrified and the heaven-dwellers trembled, beholding Kāla enraged, the bringer of fear to the three worlds.
t.7.22.7: But when the ministers of the lord of the Rākṣasas saw that monstrous chariot, accompanied by Mṛtyu, bringing terror to all the worlds,
t.7.22.8: Being weak of spirit, all of them, bereft of their senses and tormented by fear, said, "We are not able to fight here," and fled in every direction.
t.7.22.10: But Yama, enraged, closing in on Rāvaṇa and hurling spears and lances, cut into the vital parts of the rākṣasa.
t.7.22.9: But the Rākṣasa, seeing that chariot of such a kind, which brought terror to the worlds, was not shaken then, nor did any distress arise in him.
t.7.22.11: But Rāvaṇa, standing firm and composed, released a shower of arrows upon that chariot of Vaivasvata, as a rain-cloud pours down a shower of water.
t.7.22.12: Then, with hundreds of great spears being hurled down upon his mighty chest, that rākṣasa, tormented by the darts, was unable to strike back.
t.7.22.13: When the battle had thus been waged for seven nights by Yama, the crusher of foes, with weapons of many kinds, he was neither broken nor vanquished.
t.7.22.14: Then once again a battle arose there between Yama and the Rākṣasa, both longing for victory and neither ever turning back in combat.
t.7.22.15: Then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, the Siddhas and the supreme seers, placing Prajāpati at their head, beheld that battlefield.
t.7.22.16: As those two fought, the chief of the Rākṣasas and the lord of the departed spirits, it was as though the dissolution of the worlds had come to pass.
t.7.22.17: Then the lord of the Rākṣasas, enraged, drew his bow in battle and released arrows, as though making the sky one unbroken mass.
t.7.22.18: He struck Mṛtyu with four arrows and the charioteer with seven, and swiftly pierced Yama in his vital parts with a thousand arrows.
t.7.22.19: Then from the mouth of the enraged Yama there suddenly burst forth a breath garlanded with flames, the very fire of his wrath.
t.7.22.20: Then the gods, Dānavas and Rākṣasas beheld that wonder: a blazing fire born of wrath, eager to burn up the army of the foe.
t.7.22.21: Then Mṛtyu, filled with the utmost rage, said to Vaivasvata: "Release me at once, O god, and I will slay the enemy in battle."
t.7.22.23: These and many others, mighty and hard to approach, I have seen perish; what concern, then, is there over this night-wanderer?
t.7.22.22: Naraka, Śambara, Vṛtra, Śambhu, the mighty Kārttasvara, Namuci and Virocana as well, and those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
t.7.22.24: Release me, I pray, O knower of dharma, while I slay this one, for no one seen by me lives even for a moment.
t.7.22.25: This is surely not my own strength; it is a limit fixed by nature itself: whoever is touched by me cannot live, such is the certainty.
t.7.22.27: Then the lord Vaivasvata, enraged, his eyes red with fury, raised and weighed in his hand that unfailing Kāladaṇḍa.
t.7.22.26: Hearing these words, the mighty Dharmarāja then said to Mṛtyu: "Here I am; I myself shall slay him."
t.7.22.28: At its sides were set the flawless nooses of Kāla, and there stood the mace in embodied form, its touch like that of fire.
t.7.22.30: That terrible rod, wreathed in flames and seemingly enraged, touched by the hand of the mighty one, appeared as though it were drinking up the night-wanderer.
t.7.22.29: He who by his mere sight stops the life-breaths of living beings, what then need be said of his striking or crushing an embodied creature?
t.7.22.31: Then all the creatures fled from that battlefield, and the gods too were agitated, seeing Yama with the rod of Kāla raised.
t.7.22.33: O Vaivasvata, mighty-armed one of incomparable valour, you must surely not strike this night-wanderer with this rod.
t.7.22.32: But as he raised his staff, eager to strike Rāvaṇa, the Grandsire appeared in person before Yama and spoke these words.
t.7.22.35: For this Kāladaṇḍa, the Rod of Time, created by me long ago and placed under the command of Mṛtyu, is unfailing in the destruction of all creatures.
t.7.22.34: Indeed, a boon was granted to him by me, O bull among the gods; so the word that I have spoken must not be made untrue by you.
t.7.22.36: Therefore, gentle one, this must surely not be brought down by you upon the head of the rākṣasa, for when it has fallen, no one lives even for a moment.
t.7.22.37: For if, once this has fallen, this rākṣasa should not die, or if Daśagrīva should die, then either way there would be falsehood.
t.7.22.38: Restrain today this rod raised for slaying, turning it away from the lord of the Rākṣasas; and, having regard for the worlds, make this word of mine true.
t.7.22.39: Thus addressed, the righteous-souled Yama then replied: "This rod has been withdrawn, for you are our lord and master."
t.7.22.40: But what can I do now, though I have entered the battle, since this rākṣasa, made proud by his boon, is not to be slain by me?
t.7.22.41: "Therefore I shall vanish from the sight of this Rākṣasa." Having said this, he disappeared right there, together with his chariot and his horses.
t.7.22.42: Daśagrīva, having conquered him and proclaimed his own name, departed from the abode of Yama in the Puṣpaka, filled with delight.
t.7.22.43: Then Vaivasvata, rejoicing, went to the heavens together with the gods led by Brahmā, and so did the great sage Nārada.
